payload.rationale: The contract requires NASA GISS's 2026 LOTI anomaly to exceed both the 2025 value and 1.28°C (the 2024 record level), so 2026 must effectively set a new record versus the 2024 peak (~1.28°C) and 2025 (~1.2x°C). Background: 2024 was boosted by the 2023–24 El Niño; 2025 was extremely warm despite weak La Niña, showing a high baseline (~1.25°C) from the underlying ~0.2°C/decade trend plus elevated recent anomalies. Late 2025 into early 2026 featured La Niña/neutral conditions, which typically suppress the first part of the year, while seasonal outlooks earlier in 2026 pointed toward El Niño development in the second half of 2026. El Niño mainly boosts global temperature with a several-month lag, so most of that boost would land in late 2026 and 2027. Pre-season outlooks (e.g., Met Office, Berkeley Earth style forecasts) generally placed 2026 among the top three years with a meaningful but sub-even chance of a record. Because 2024's first half was exceptionally hot, 2026 would need a strong late-year surge to overtake it. I have no observed 2026 monthly data, so I center near 0.35. Too high if: El Niño failed to develop or is weak, early-2026 months ran well below 2024, or the record margin needed (>1.28 and >2025) is larger than recent-year variability allows. Too low if: a rapid, strong El Niño emerged by mid-2026 together with the persistently elevated post-2023 baseline (low aerosols, high ocean heat), making late-2026 months record-hot and pushing the annual mean above ~1.29–1.30°C; 2023 showed an onset-year record is possible.
limitations: No supplied evidence; no access to 2026 monthly GISS data or current ENSO state as of the cutoff.
Exact 2025 GISS annual value and its relation to the 1.28°C threshold assumed from memory.
ENSO evolution through 2026 and its lagged temperature effect are uncertain.
GISS annual value may be revised; only the first reported value likely matters for settlement.
